focus: Use multiplication facts to 10 × 10 and their related division facts. An array shows equal rows and columns; turning it preserves the total.
Build a less familiar fact from known facts: double, halve, split groups, or add or remove one whole group. Explain what each part counts.
Extend facts to larger mental calculations without a calculator. Keep track of tens and hundreds, and check using the inverse relationship.
AC9M4A02.model_alt: Six rows of counters, each split into two blue counters and five gold counters.
AC9M4A02.model_caption: Split 7 columns into 2 and 5. The parts contain 6 × 2 = 12 and 6 × 5 = 30 counters, so 6 × 7 = 42.
AC9M4A02.example: Use 6 × 7 = 42 to find 60 × 7: sixty is six tens, so the result is 42 tens, or 420. The inverse check is 420 ÷ 7 = 60. For 23 × 4, split 23 into 20 and 3: 80 + 12 = 92.
AC9M4A02.mistake: One more group of 8 adds 8, not 1. When you use a fact with tens, keep the tens unit in the answer.
AC9M4A02.materials: Have paper, a pencil and small paper cards ready. Drawing and game tasks require your actual work; an adult checks the array, calculations, rules and recorded play before awarding credit.
AC9M4A02.review: Name the known fact that helped, explain your strategy and check a related division fact. Accept a different strategy when every step is correct.

focus: Choose the attribute, instrument and unit: length, mass, capacity, duration or temperature. Read the unit on a digital display as well as the digits.
On a scale, find two labelled values and count the equal intervals between them. Divide their difference by the number of intervals to find each step.
Read whole and part units carefully. Estimate between marks only as precisely as the instrument allows, and explain how you checked the measurement.
AC9M4M01.model_alt: A mass scale runs from 200 grams to 500 grams in six equal intervals. The pointer is three intervals after 200 grams.
AC9M4M01.model_caption: The labelled difference is 300 g across 6 equal intervals. Each interval is 50 g, so the pointer reads 200 g + 150 g = 350 g.
AC9M4M01.example: A thermometer has five equal intervals from 20 °C to 30 °C. Each interval is 2 °C, so the third interval above 20 °C reads 26 °C. If an object's ends line up with 2 cm and 9 cm on a ruler, its length is 9 − 2 = 7 cm.
AC9M4M01.mistake: Count spaces between marks, not the marks themselves. A timer showing 02:35 in minutes:seconds means 2 minutes 35 seconds, not 2.35 minutes.
AC9M4M01.materials: Some tasks need a ruler, a measuring jug, a timer or other named instrument. Prepare the equipment with an adult or complete the task in class. Record the actual measurement and unit; an adult checks practical work before awarding credit.
AC9M4M01.review: Explain the value of one interval, the starting reading and the pointer position. For a made instrument, compare several readings with a trusted instrument.

focus: State the starting and finishing times, including am or pm and the day. Count forward in useful jumps through the next hour, noon or midnight.
Use 60 seconds = 1 minute and 60 minutes = 1 hour. Use groups of 60 when converting between these units, not groups of 100.
When planning a timetable, include activities, rests and any waiting time. Public cultural accounts can explain repeating Sun, Moon and star cycles; identify the particular community and source.
AC9M4M03.model_alt: Friday timeline: 11:45 am to 12 noon is a 15-minute jump; noon to 12:25 pm is a 25-minute jump.
AC9M4M03.model_caption: The two jumps cross noon on Friday: 15 minutes + 25 minutes = 40 minutes altogether. Noon is 12 pm.
AC9M4M03.example: From 11:40 pm on Monday to 12:15 am on Tuesday, count 20 minutes to midnight, then 15 minutes: 35 minutes. To convert 2 minutes 35 seconds, calculate 2 × 60 + 35 = 155 seconds.
AC9M4M03.mistake: 12 noon is 12 pm; midnight is 12 am and starts a new day. Do not treat 1 hour 30 minutes as 130 minutes: it is 60 + 30 = 90 minutes.
AC9M4M03.materials: Have paper and a pencil ready for timelines and schedules. Written planning tasks need all activity times and any rests; an adult checks your completed work before awarding credit.
AC9M4M03.review: Add the duration back to the start and check that you reach the stated finish on the correct day. Check conversions with groups of 60.

focus: Compare the indicated opening or turn with a right angle. Acute is smaller than a right angle; obtuse is larger than a right angle and smaller than a straight angle.
A straight angle is two right angles. A reflex angle is greater than a straight angle and less than a full revolution. One revolution is four right angles.
Arm length and page orientation do not change angle size. Align a checked right-angle template at the vertex and along one arm; follow the marked arc to identify the intended angle.
AC9M4M04.model_alt: An arrow turns anticlockwise from an upward arm through three quarters of a circle to a rightward arm.
AC9M4M04.model_caption: The marked turn is three right angles. It is greater than a straight angle and less than a revolution, so it is reflex.
AC9M4M04.example: On a top-view sketch of an open door, place a right-angle template at the drawn hinge, with one edge along the closed position. If the marked opening is wider than the template but less than a half turn, it is obtuse. Check the indicated opening, because the same arms also enclose a different angle around the other side.
AC9M4M04.mistake: Longer arms do not make a larger angle. A spirit level checks level or plumb using the appropriate vial; use a set square or a checked right-angle template to compare a corner with a right angle.
AC9M4M04.materials: Prepare a pencil, separate paper, folding paper or card, a checked right-angle template and the tools named in a practical task. Arrange set-square or spirit-level work with an adult or in class. Complete the actual task before asking an adult to check it.
AC9M4M04.review: Point to the vertex and marked opening, compare it with right-angle turns, and explain how a template or suitable tool supports your conclusion.

focus: Perimeter measures the whole boundary using length units. Area measures the enclosed surface using square units or other equal area units.
Count boundary lengths for perimeter and covered tiles for area. Fit area units without gaps or overlaps; combine part units when a boundary cuts through a tile.
Choose formal or informal units that suit the space. State when a result is approximate, and explain your measuring method.
AC9M4M02.model_alt: A rectangle has six columns and four rows of square tiles. Each tile side is one length unit. Orange outlines only the outer boundary.
AC9M4M02.model_caption: The boundary is 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 length units. The surface contains 4 rows of 6 tiles, so its area is 24 square units.
AC9M4M02.example: If a region covers 12 whole grid squares and 6 half-squares, pair the halves to make 3 whole squares. The area is 12 + 3 = 15 square units. For a curved boundary, fit string around the complete edge once, mark the meeting point, then straighten and measure the string.
AC9M4M02.mistake: Do not add internal grid lines to the perimeter or count boundary lengths as area. The same area can have different perimeters. For the same length or area, smaller units give a larger count.
AC9M4M02.materials: Have paper, a pencil, a ruler, string and one paper square ready for practical tasks. Use separate paper when a diagram needs more room. An adult checks actual measuring, drawings and explanations before awarding credit; a printed picture is not a calibrated ruler.
AC9M4M02.review: Trace the complete boundary for perimeter. For area, check how the units cover the surface and how part units combine. Include the unit and explain any estimate.
